To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) A compact state representation, learned by a vector quantizer that grows its dictionary size over the course of training, can be used to improve performance in reinforcement learning; 2) This representation can be learned jointly with the policy, in a manner that allows for a compact neural network; 3) The resulting system can be used to learn policies for Atari games using only 6 neurons, and achieves comparable results to the state of the art, while being much easier to understand and interpret

(1) we have developed a new algorithm that learns compact state representations in an open ended, online setting; (2) we have developed an extension of the Exponential NES algorithm which adapts the probability distribution dimensionality to the size of the neural network inputs; and (3) we have shown that our algorithm is capable of producing state of the art results on Atari games with tiny neural networks.

we propose a new algorithm for learning compact state representations, that we propose a novel algorithm for training tiny neural networks, and that we show that these two techniques together can be applied to deep reinforcement learning, and can achieve comparable results with much smaller networks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether we can understand the internal representation of a deep neural network, and how to make it more interpretable and generalizable.

the following questions: Can we learn policies with a very small number of neurons? Can we learn state representations which capture all relevant information? Can we learn both simultaneously, and online?
the question of how to best represent the state of a system, in order to achieve a good policy for its control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we are able to show a significant reduction of the neural network size in a vision based reinforcement learning problem, while achieving comparable or superior performance to state of the arts.
our method is capable of learning state representations and policies for Atari games with very few neurons and a very simple architecture.
the proposed system is capable of achieving results competitive with state of the art, while being much more interpretable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that it is possible to learn policies and compact state encoders in a joint manner, without any prior knowledge about the environment, in order to achieve results comparable or better than the current state of the art.

the system learns to learn: it is capable of adapting to new observations, new tasks and new policies, while still being capable of achieving state of the art results on a wide variety of Atari games, and even on a novel game.
the combination of the three proposed methods allows for learning compact policies and state representations in a fully online manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to learn compact policies and representations simultaneously and autonomously.
it is indeed possible to learn a policy and a state representation in an end to end fashion, while keeping the state representation small enough to be interpretable.
it is possible to learn policies for vision based tasks with very little information, as long as it's possible to extract the right features.
